Jasmin Orth | Philipp Mondorf | Barbara Plank Conditional acceptability refers to how plausible a conditional statement is perceived to be. It plays an important role in communication and reasoning, as it influences how individuals interpret implications, assess arguments, and make decisions based on hypothetical scenarios. When humans evaluate how acceptable a conditional “If A, then B” is, their judgments are influenced by two main factors: the conditional probability of B given A , and the semantic relevance of the antecedent A given the consequent B (i.e., whether A meaningfully supports B ). While prior work has examined how large language models (LLMs) draw inferences about conditional statements, it remains unclear how these models judge the acceptability of such statements. To address this gap, we present a comprehensive study of LLMs’ conditional acceptability judgments across different model families, sizes, and prompting strategies. Using linear mixed-effects models and ANOVA tests, we find that models are sensitive to both conditional probability and semantic relevance — though to varying degrees depending on architecture and prompting style. A comparison with human data reveals that while LLMs incorporate probabilistic and semantic cues, they do so less consistently than humans. Contradiction detection is a focused subtask that identifies when two statements cannot simultaneously be true under the same interpretation. Contradictions can occur either within a single document (self-contradictions) or across multiple documents on related content (pairwise contradictions). In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), unresolved conflicts like outdated statutes, overlapping jurisdictions, or inconsistent interpretations can lead models to produce factually incorrect or logically inconsistent outputs. Left unfiltered, these contradictions represent a high-risk form of hallucination in legal and policy settings. Despite growing interest, existing contradiction benchmarks are poorly suited for stress-testing generative systems. Early work in NLI introduced datasets like SNLI [Bowman et al., 2015], MNLI [Williams et al., 2017], and ANLI [Williams et al., 2020], but these focus on isolated sentence pairs and lack the linguistic and structural complexity of real documents. More domain-specific resources such as ContractNLI [Koreeda and Manning, 2021] are limited to clause-level reasoning. ContraDoc [Li et al., 2023] and ECON [Jiayang et al., 2024] move toward document- and retrieval- scale evaluation. ContraDoc showed that even GPT-4 struggles with subtle internal inconsistencies in long documents, and that trained annotators also miss many contradictions. ECON distinguishes factoid and answer conflicts, showing that models often default to internal priors when evidence is inconsistent. Gokul et al. extend this work to synthetic RAG pipelines by generating controlled contradictions and testing LLMs as context validators, but consider only three types: self, pairwise, and conditional. exa-lite.snippet:
###### Abstract

A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent’s own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent’s family of large language models.

> Abstract:Argumentation is an important cognitive activity that involves the scrutiny of arguments and counterarguments. When given an argument, it is desirable that its premises entail its claim, and that the premises and claim are consistent, and when given a pair of arguments, it is desirable to check whether one argument supports or attacks another. If the arguments are in natural language, then we could use methods for natural language inference, also known as recognizing textual entailment (RTE). The state-of-the-art RTE methods use machine learning and deep learning, but these are not explainable. An alternative approach which we investigate in this paper is to translate text into an abstract meaning representation (AMR) graph. For this we use a pre-trained AMR parser. We then translate the AMR graph into propositional logic and use a SAT solver for automated reasoning. In text, often common sense suggests that an entailment (or contradiction) relationship holds between a premise and a claim, but because different wordings are used, this is not identified from their logical representations. To address this, we introduce relaxation methods to allow replacement or forgetting of some propositions. Our experimental results show our approach performs well on three RTE datasets. The benefit of our approach is that we have a logical representation of premises and claims, and of the relaxations that are used to identify the entailment and contradiction relations.

###### Abstract

New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher’s computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

jina.snippet:
## **How to design, build, and evaluate what your agent actually sees.**

[![Image 1: Youssef Hosni](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*Wftd4SJciOP8CoW3xJqeJQ.jpeg)](https://yousefhosni.medium.com/?source=post_page---byline--b2738c85a7fd------------------------------------------)

87 min read

Sep 21, 2026

An AI agent can start with clear instructions and the right tools, yet struggle as a task progresses. Search results accumulate, tool calls return pages of data, and earlier assumptions remain in the conversation after new evidence has replaced them. At each step, the agent must work through this growing history to find what matters for its next decision. This guide takes you through the concepts, implementation, and evaluation of that process. We begin with the components of agent context, the ways context can fail, and four core operations: **Write, Select, Compress, and Isolate**.

We then build a research agent with the **Claude Agent SDK**, starting with a naive baseline and progressively adding persistent working state…

keenable.title: From Correctness to Consistency: Redefining Reliability for the Agentware Era
keenable.snippet:
The rise of “vibe coding” has marginalized requirement analysis, allowing unverified “Make it Work” assumptions to accumulate into complex defects that evade standard testing. Preliminary simulations demonstrate that DLA successfully intercepts logic drift, such as contradictions and unspecified assumptions, and offers a new perspective on reliability assessment in the AI-assistant development era.

keenable.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
keenable.snippet:
However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. keenable.title: From Tool to Teammate: LLM Coding Agents as Collaborative Partners for Behavioral Labeling in Educational Dialogue Analysis
keenable.snippet:

Continued iteration beyond the optimum led to regression, underscoring the need for held-out validation.

Every team that ships an LLM-powered tool hits the same wall. The demo works. The first real workload doesn’t. The model isn’t the problem — the architecture is.

Then the team routes a full day’s tickets: 200 support requests ranging from order tracking to refund disputes to technical troubleshooting. The agent needs to check order histories, apply return policies, cross-reference warranty terms, and draft personalized resolutions. Title: Hidden in Plain Sight: an Empirical Study about The Instruction Stacks of Coding Agents

Authors: Felipe de Sant'Anna Paixão, Dhyego Tavares, Eduardo Almeida, Iftekhar Ahmed

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Coding agents send their models more than the user's prompt: they add instructions, tool definitions, and environmental context that form an instruction stack. This stack guides execution and changes across releases, yet remains largely unexposed to users and insufficiently characterized in research. We present a longitudinal, cross-agent study of the instruction stacks captured in the first model requests of 1,886 releases of Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, and OpenCode. Under controlled conditions, we analyze their composition and evolution and trace changes in the four open-source agents to documented motivations. Our findings show why examining the system prompt or reporting the model alone provides an incomplete account of agent inputs. Tool definitions dominate three agents' latest requests, while occasional concentrated revisions alter instructions governing tool use, attribution, and coding style. Such revisions can complicate how researchers identify agent-authored contributions and interpret generated code. We also found that only 48% of examined change units directly explain the motivation for stack revisions. Across agents, shared capabilities emerge despite increasingly distinct wording. These findings expose an evolving, incompletely documented layer of agent design. The findings motivate documenting captured instruction stacks alongside agent releases, models, and user prompts, and preserving the rationale behind their revisions.

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: The deployment of LLM-based agents in scientific analysis raises opposing concerns: that agents may reduce methodological diversity, or that they may amplify the analytic flexibility through which researchers reach motivated conclusions. We argue these worries target two empirically separable layers: a design layer of methodological choices, and a verdict layer in which a decision rule maps estimates to a substantive claim. We test both by running 20 independent executions of Claude Code and Codex on a prominent immigration and social-policy against a many-analysts human baseline. At the design layer, Codex matches human methodological diversity and Claude Code produces nearly three times as many specifications; both agents' effect estimates remain broadly aligned with the human consensus, and no agent model exactly matches any human model. A prompt-induced anti-immigration researcher prior reorganizes each agent's methodological decisions but, unlike for biased human analysts in the same data, does not shift aggregate estimates or final verdicts; nor do agents reroute along the methodological axes humans use to bias their estimates. At the verdict layer, an explicit confirmatory prompt flips Claude Code's verdicts from 10% to 90% support while leaving its coefficient distribution essentially unchanged, operating through rule omission rather than rule softening. AI agents can rival or exceed human methodological diversity at the design layer while remaining vulnerable at the verdict layer. In our setting, the locus of AI bias is not estimation but interpretation.

A same-model control establishes that even with no capability gap, independent re-extraction from identical text agrees only 59.3% of the time. ## What Is an Agentic Coding Workflow?

An agentic coding workflow is a development loop where AI coding agents do the work end to end. They plan a change, read the codebase, write and edit multiple files, run tests, and open a pull request, while a human engineer sets intent, reviews, and signs off.

That is the whole distinction from AI autocomplete. Autocomplete predicts the next token or the next few lines inside the file you are editing. It is reactive and single-turn. You stay in the driver seat keystroke by keystroke. An agentic coding workflow takes a scoped goal and drives the full plan-build-test-ship loop. Autocomplete finishes your sentence. An agent ships the feature.

Anthropic frames its own tool the same way. As the Claude Code best practices put it, \"Claude Code is an agentic coding environment. Unlike a chatbot that answers questions and waits, Claude Code can read your files, run commands, make changes, and autonomously work through problems while you watch, redirect, or step away entirely.\"

The human role changes with it. Instead of writing the code and asking the model to review it, you describe the outcome and the agent explores, plans, and implements. ## Why multi-agent prompt engineering matters in 2026

Most prompt-engineering advice assumes a single model, a single user, and a single turn. But 2026 is the year production AI leans into teams of specialized agents working together. In multi-agent systems, language models don’t just answer—they plan, delegate, negotiate, retrieve evidence, call tools, and check one another’s work. # Contradiction Retrieval Methods. * Contradiction retrieval is an automated technique that identifies mutually exclusive claims using three-class textual entailment frameworks. * It leverages features like vocabulary overlap, POS similarity, and local alignment to differentiate entailment, contradiction, and neutrality with measurable performance metrics. The capability to distinguish and retrieve contradictions is foundational for tasks including misinformation detection, fact-checking, automated reasoning, and the maintenance of semantic consistency across both structured knowledge systems and open-domain corpora. Such formalization enables generic models to process a wide variety of contradiction expressions without explicit extraction of claim targets or conversational structures. Statistical analysis across these features consistently reveals that entailment pairs yield higher similarity and alignment scores, with contradictions displaying lower and overlapping distributions (Kruskal–Wallis and Dunnett post-hoc tests confirm statistical significance). ultimate.title: From Correctness to Consistency: Redefining Reliability for the Agentware Era
ultimate.snippet:
The rise of “vibe coding” has marginalized requirement analysis, allowing unverified “Make it Work” assumptions to accumulate into complex defects that evade standard testing. In the absence of a reliable ground truth oracle, we advocate a paradigm shift from correctness verification to logic consistency. We introduce Differential Logic Analysis (DLA), a framework that utilizes Logical Inference to detect internal contradictions across parallel and sequential development workflows. Preliminary simulations demonstrate that DLA successfully intercepts logic drift, such as contradictions and unspecified assumptions, and offers a new perspective on reliability assessment in the AI-assistant development era.

To answer the questions, we conducted two case studies: 1) Parallel Development: Where multiple agents independently implement related features, creating the potential for logic divergence (Huth and Ryan, 2004) in isolation (e.g., assumptions made by agents work locally but conflict globally). 2) Sequential Iteration: Where a single agent refines a codebase over multiple turns, creating the potential for logic drift over iterations (e.g., new-turn logic diverges from prior logic). We then manually applied DLA rules to the artifacts generated in these simulations. By treating the natural language prompts and code segments as logical premises, we tested whether Logical Inference, specifically Entailment (logical consequence), Contradiction, and Neutrality (MacCartney and Manning, 2008), could successfully contextualize software logic. Our analysis confirmed that DLA could systematically identify “logic divergence” and “unspecified assumptions” that auto-generated tests failed to catch, proving that Logic Consistency is a viable and measurable proxy for reliability in the absence of a ground truth.

ultimate.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
ultimate.snippet:
Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently
across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools,
produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability
compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation
metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not
capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior
is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-
response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency
propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic
Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation
metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic
disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same
state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined
recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on
independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the
current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full
trajectory to complete.

ultimate.title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
ultimate.snippet:
Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders
to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features con-
nected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight
requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an
off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored
skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading
the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant
proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowl-
edge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level
interventions.

ultimate.title: Retromorphic Testing with Hierarchical Verification for Hallucination Detection in RAG
ultimate.snippet: Large language models can still hallucinate in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), producing claims that are unsupported by or conflict with the retrieved context. Detecting such errors remains challenging when faithfulness is judged solely against the retrieved context: many existing detectors return holistic answer-level scores, while others target open-domain factuality or fail to provide evidence-grounded diagnostics. We present RT4CHART, a retromorphic testing framework for context-faithfulness assessment that decomposes an answer into independently verifiable claims, performs hierarchical local-to-global verification against the retrieved context, and assigns each claim one of three labels—entailed, contradicted, or baseless. RT4CHART further maps these claim-level decisions back to specific answer spans and returns explicit context-side evidence, enabling fine-grained auditing rather than opaque scoring.

ultimate.title: The Imperfective Paradox in Large Language Models
ultimate.snippet:
We investigate the Imperfective Paradox, a logical phenomenon where the past progressive aspect entails event realization for activities (e.g., running → ran) but not for accomplishments (e.g., building ↛ built). We introduce ImperfectiveNLI, a diagnostic dataset designed to probe this distinction across diverse semantic classes. Evaluating state-of-the-art open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Teleological Bias: models systematically hallucinate completion for goal-oriented events, even overriding explicit textual cancellation. Prompting interventions partially reduce this bias but trigger a calibration crisis, causing models to incorrectly reject valid entailments for atelic verbs. Representational analyses further show that while internal embeddings often distinguish progressive from simple past forms, inference decisions are dominated by strong priors about goal attainment. Taken together, our findings indicate that these current open-weight LLMs operate as predictive narrative engines rather than faithful logical reasoners, and that resolving aspectual inference requires moving beyond prompting toward structurally grounded alignment.11

ultimate.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
ultimate.snippet:
However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present VerifyAgent, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs. 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], p=5.82×10^(−8)) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0% vs. 15.4%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta (Δℬ) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0% vs. 62.5% for Fixed-3) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4×.

To address these challenges, we present VerifyAgent, an agentic verification system built on two core design principles: (1) structurally decouple the *evaluator* from the *generator* via divergent epistemic mandates and real-time representation monitoring, so that verification cannot ratify its own priors; and (2) define convergence as a measurable, artifact-grounded stabilization of the belief state rather than model self-reported confidence.

ultimate.title: From Tool to Teammate: LLM Coding Agents as Collaborative Partners for Behavioral Labeling in Educational Dialogue Analysis
ultimate.snippet:
Behavioral analysis of tutoring dialogues is essential for understanding student learning, yet manual coding remains a bottleneck. We present a methodology where LLM coding agents autonomously improve the prompts used by LLM classifiers to label educational dialogues. In each iteration, a coding agent runs the classifier against human-labeled validation data, analyzes disagreements, and proposes theory-grounded prompt modifications for researcher review. Applying this approach to 659 AI tutoring sessions across four experiments with three agents and three classifiers, 4-fold cross-validation on held-out data confirmed genuine improvement: the best agent achieved test κ=0.78 (SD=0.08), matching human inter-rater reliability (κ=0.78), at a cost of approximately $5–8 per agent. While development-set performance reached κ=0.91–0.93, the cross-validated results represent our primary generalization claim. The iterative process also surfaced an undocumented labeling pattern: human coders consistently treated expressions of confusion as engagement rather than disengagement. Continued iteration beyond the optimum led to regression, underscoring the need for held-out validation.

We present an alternative approach where LLM coding agents serve not as tools to be configured, but as research teammates that autonomously iterate on labeling prompts through systematic error analysis. Applying this methodology to behavioral labeling in AI tutoring dialogues, we address practical questions: How many iterations are needed?
